bib.title: Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances", Ahn, Brohan, Brown, Chebotar, ... Ichter, Xia, Hausman, ... Zeng (Robotics at Google, Everyday Robots; authors listed alphabetically). The extracted file is arXiv:2204.01691v2 [cs.RO], 16 Aug 2022. It has no venue line. I could not confirm CoRL 2022 from this text, so cite it as a preprint, or check the venue somewhere else.

COVERAGE: I read all 109,709 of 109,709 chars, pages 1–34, including the appendices (prompts, Tables 5–8, failure figures). I skimmed the references for origins only.

CLAIMS
- claim: The paper scores the system with two separate metrics. Plan success asks whether the chosen skills are right, whether or not they executed. Execution success asks whether the robot actually did the task. Both are judged by 3 human raters, and 2 of 3 must agree.
  number: 3 raters, 2-of-3 majority
  setup: all 101 instructions; plan raters look at the generated plan, execution raters watch the robot
  quote: "We ask 3 human raters to indicate whether the plan generated by the model can achieve the instruction, and if 2 out of 3 raters agree that the plan is valid, it is marked a success. Note that for many instructions there may be multiple valid solutions." / "We ask 3 human raters to watch the robot execution... We mark an execution successful if 2 out of 3 raters agree that it is successful."
  where: p7, Metrics
- claim: The headline result is a gap between plan and execution, and it gets wider in the real kitchen.
  number: mock kitchen 84% plan / 74% execute; real kitchen 81% / 60%
  setup: PaLM 540B, 101 instructions, mobile manipulator, 15 objects, 5 locations; the mock kitchen is also where the skills were trained
  quote: "PaLM-SayCan achieves a planning success rate of 84% and execution success rate of 74% in the training environment and 81% planning and 60% execution in a real kitchen."
  where: p9, Table 2 caption
- claim: The evaluation set is 101 instructions in 7 families. They were built to test separate abilities, drawing on Mechanical Turk, in-person kitchen users, ALFRED and BEHAVIOR.
  number: 101 instructions; 15 per family except Embodiment, which has 11
  setup: families are NL Single Primitive, NL Nouns, NL Verbs, Structured Language, Embodiment, Crowd-Sourced and Long-Horizon. Plans range "from single primitives to 10+ in a row"
  quote: "we test across 101 instructions from 7 instruction families, summarized in Table 1"
  where: p6
- claim: Results per family, plan/execute, mock kitchen. Long-Horizon and NL Nouns lose the most between plan and execution. Structured Language is a deliberate ablation that mirrors NL Verbs.
  number: Single 100/100, Nouns 67/47, Verbs 100/93, Structured 93/87, Embodiment 64/55, Crowd 87/87, Long-Horizon 73/47
  setup: Table 2, PaLM-SayCan
  quote: "Long-Horizon 15 73% 47% 73% 47% 67% 60% 0% 0%"
  where: p9, Table 2
- claim: Errors were classified by source. About two-thirds came from the LLM and one-third from affordances (perception). Long-horizon failures were mostly early termination.
  number: 65% LLM / 35% affordance
  setup: errors across the 101-task evaluation
  quote: "most failures were a result of early termination by the LLM (e.g., bringing one object but not the second)... Overall, 65% of the errors were LLM failures and 35% were affordance failures."
  where: p8
- claim: Removing the affordance (value function) grounding lowers plan success. Embodiment tasks suffer most.
  number: No VF 67%, Generative 74%, SayCan 84% planning; Embodiment 18% (No VF) and 36% (Gen) vs 64%
  setup: same 101 instructions. No VF takes the highest LLM-scored skill. Generative uses free text projected to skills by USE cosine similarity, close to Huang et al. 2022
  quote: "The No VF and Generative approaches performed similarly, achieving 67% and 74% planning success rate respectively, and worse than PaLM-SayCan's 84%."
  where: p8; Table 2 p9
- claim: Removing the LLM leaves almost nothing working.
  number: BC NL 0%; BC USE 60% on single primitives, 9% overall
  setup: the policy receives the raw instruction (BC NL), or the instruction projected to the nearest known command (BC USE)
  quote: "BC NL achieves 0% in all tasks and BC USE achieves 60% for single primitives, but 0% otherwise."
  where: p8
- claim: Swapping in a better LLM improves end-to-end robot success. The authors call this the first time an LLM gain has visibly carried through to robotics.
  number: PaLM 84/74 vs FLAN 137B 70/61 (plan/execute)
  setup: full SayCan, 101 instructions
  quote: "SayCan achieves a planning success rate of 84% and execution success rate of 74% with PaLM and FLAN achieves 70% planning and 61% success."
  where: p9, Table 3
- claim: Scaling the model, measured without the value function (generative plus USE).
  number: PaLM 540B 74%, 62B 72%, 8B 38%, FLAN 137B 43%
  setup: Table 6, generative outputs only
  quote: "Total 101 74% 72% 38% 43%"
  where: p29, Table 6
- claim: Adding a skill can give perfect plans while execution stays poor, because the low-level manipulation fails.
  number: 100% plan, 33% execution
  setup: drawer skills, "Over 21 queries"; Table 7 lists 3 instructions
  quote: "Over 21 queries we found a planning rate of 100% and an execution rate of 33% (due to failures of the chained manipulation policy)"
  where: p10; Table 7 p29
- claim: How the number of prompt examples affects planning. This was measured in a language-only simulator, not on the robot.
  number: 0 examples 10% (52% if termination not required); 4 examples 82%; 17 examples 88%
  setup: 50 instructions in the "language-based simulator", which takes a query and solution and generates affordances plus distractors
  quote: "With no examples SayCan is able to successfully plan 54% without the done condition, but only 10% with the done condition... After only four examples the LLM is performant, planning 82%... involved 17 examples and recovered 88%"
  where: p24, Table 5 p25 (the text says 54%, Table 5 says 52%)
- claim: Multilingual planning barely drops. One French query failed.
  number: 11 of 12 queries planned at 1.0
  setup: 3 English queries translated into Chinese, French and Spanish; plan rate only
  quote: "there is almost no performance drop on planning success rate when changing the queries from English to Chinese, French and Spanish"
  where: p30, Table 8
- claim: Human raters also produce the training reward. They watch a video of each skill episode, and 2 of 3 must agree.
  number: 2 of 3 raters
  setup: sparse 0/1 reward for skill training
  quote: "If two out of the three raters agree that the skill was accomplished successfully, the episode is labelled with a positive reward."
  where: p5
- claim: Skill policies were iterated on a separate evaluation protocol in the mock kitchen before being "graduated" to the real kitchen.
  number: 366 real-world model evaluations; 50-action cap per episode
  setup: a human operator records success or failure per episode
  quote: "from 1 instruction in April 2021 to hundreds of instructions at time of publication over the course of 366 real-world model evaluations"
  where: p22

LIMITS
- The paper never says how many execution trials were run per instruction, so the per-family percentages over 15 items are likely single runs. It reports no variance and no confidence intervals. No inter-rater agreement statistic is given beyond the 2-of-3 rule.
- The authors concede that SayCan inherits LLM biases, and that the main bottleneck is "the range and capabilities of the underlying skills". They also say the system "is not easily able to react to situations where individual skills fail despite reporting a high value" because it is open-loop. Inner Monologue (Huang et al. [25]) adds closed-loop feedback.
- It struggles with negation and ambiguous references, such as "drinks with caffeine". Chain-of-thought is shown only in qualitative rollouts (Table 4), with no numbers.
- Navigation assumes object locations are known. Place is scripted with an affordance fixed at 1.0. The value functions need hand calibration (pick min 0.2, max 0.5).
- The prompt ablation runs on a language simulator, not the robot.
- It is dated: PaLM/FLAN-era models, the scoring interface needs log-probs, and it uses a single fixed kitchen.

BUILDS ON: BC-Z (Jang et al. 2021); MT-Opt (Kalashnikov et al. 2021); Universal Sentence Encoder (Cer et al. 2018); RetinaGAN (Ho et al. 2021); Value function spaces (Shah et al. 2022); affordances (Gibson 1977); PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022); FLAN (Wei et al. 2021); Chain of thought (Wei et al. 2022); Huang et al. 2022, zero-shot planners (the concurrent work, matching the Generative baseline); ALFRED (Shridhar et al. 2020) and BEHAVIOR (Srivastava et al. 2022), which inspired the instructions.

CODE
- Algorithm 1 (p5), core selection: "pcombinedπ = paffordanceπ pLLMπ ... πn = arg maxπ∈Π C", looping until "done". The factorisation (p3) is "p(ci|i,s,𝓁π)∝p(cπ|s,𝓁π)p(𝓁π|i)", which is task-grounding × world-grounding.
- Prompt format (Listing 1, p25): "Human: How would you bring me an orange?\nRobot: 1. find an orange, 2. pick up the orange, 3. bring it to you, 4. put down the orange, 5. done."
- Affordance for terminate (p24): "paffordanceterminate = 0.1".

FIGURES
- Fig. 3 / 13 (p5, p23): LLM scores × value-function scores combined to pick a skill. It shows the Say × Can product faster than the equations do.
- Fig. 6 / 14 (p8, p31): per-step bar charts of LLM, affordance and combined scores. These show plan interpretability and how a trace can be audited.
- Fig. 16 (p33): failure cases, split into affordance misses and LLM early termination, with the 65/35 error split in the caption. Useful for teaching error attribution in agent evals.
- Table 2 (p9): the plan-vs-execute, per-family and ablation grid in one place. It is the core eval artifact.

PROBLEMS
- Figures 6, 14 and 16 extract as glyph garbage (e.g. "+XPDQ,VSLOOHG"). Captions are fine. I decoded the content only where the captions state it.
- Table numbering is wrong in the source. Two tables are labelled "Table 5": the prompt-examples table and the full instruction list. Section 5.1 says per-instruction results are in "Appendix Table 5", but that table lists only instructions, with no results.
- The text says 54% for 0 examples without termination, while Table 5 shows 52%.
- The text says "Over 21 queries" for the drawer tasks, but Table 7 rates (0.83, 0.17) imply 6 trials per instruction (18 total), so the counts are inconsistent.
- Table 6 (540B = 74%) uses the generative + USE setup, not full SayCan. Do not quote it as SayCan's score.
- No embedded instructions were found.
- Working copy of the extraction: /tmp/saycan.txt. Source: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/ahn-2022-do-as-i-can-not.pdf
